item.title: Trump arrives in Philippines for ASEAN Summit, will meet Quad leaders
item.description: US President Donald Trump arrived in Manila on Tuesday (local time) to participate in the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and hold discussions with leaders of the Quad ...
item.content:encoded:
Trump arrives in Philippines for ASEAN Summit, will meet Quad leaders US President Donald Trump arrived in Manila on Tuesday (local time) to participate in the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and hold discussions with leaders of the Quad grouping, amid continuing geopolitical tensions and growing focus on Indo-Pacific security. ANI | Updated: 17-11-2026 15:35 IST | Created: 17-11-2026 15:35 IST

US President Donald Trump arrives in Manila (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US President Donald Trump arrived in Manila on Tuesday (local time) to participate in the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and hold discussions with leaders of the Quad grouping, amid continuing geopolitical tensions and growing focus on Indo-Pacific security. Upon his arrival, Trump was welcomed by Philippine Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, Ilocos Norte Representative and presidential son Sandro Marcos, Philippine Ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel Romualdez, US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton and Pasay City Mayor Emi Calixto.' Marching bands and young performers awaited Trump's arrival at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport's (NAIA) Balagbag Ramp on Tuesday afternoon as part of the reception arrangements. Trump's arrival in the Philippines marks the first leg of his multi-day Asia visit, during which he is expected to engage with regional leaders on security, trade and strategic cooperation. On Tuesday, the US President is scheduled to participate in a meeting with Quad leaders from India, Japan and Australia to discuss security in the Indo-Pacific region. According to the White House itinerary, the meeting will mark the first in-person Quad leaders' summit in two years and Trump's first such engagement during his current presidential term. The Quad, comprising India, the United States, Japan and Australia, is a diplomatic partnership that focuses on cooperation across areas including maritime security, regional stability, critical and emerging technologies and economic resilience. Ahead of his departure for Asia on Monday, Trump described the visit as a "big trip" while speaking to reporters and indicated the possibility of meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his visit to Asia. During his Philippines engagements, Trump is also scheduled to sign a trade agreement with Thailand and attend a dinner with Southeast Asian and other regional leaders. The 49th ASEAN Summit is being held in the Philippines from November 15 to 17, bringing together leaders from Southeast Asia and partner countries to discuss regional and international developments. The Philippines' chairmanship has placed particular emphasis on maritime security, regional stability and negotiations between ASEAN and China over a Code of Conduct for the South China Sea. The summit comes at a time of heightened geopolitical developments in the Indo-Pacific, with regional countries seeking to strengthen cooperation on maritime security, economic partnerships and strategic challenges. Trump's participation in the ASEAN and Quad engagements also comes amid continuing international tensions, including the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the situation involving the United States and Iran. Following his engagements in Manila, Trump is scheduled to hold a state visit and attend a lunch banquet hosted by Philippine President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. at the presidential palace on Wednesday. He will subsequently depart for Shenzhen, China, where he is scheduled to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit. On Thursday, Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the summit, with discussions expected to cover major international issues, including Iran and nuclear non-proliferation. (ANI)

item.title: Spanish journalist Karlos Zurutuza highlights media blackout, risks to reporters covering Balochistan at Germany conference
item.description: Spanish journalist Karlos Zurutuza has raised concerns over the limited international media coverage of Balochistan, highlighting the challenges faced by foreign correspondents and the growing risks ...
item.content:encoded:
Spanish journalist Karlos Zurutuza highlights media blackout, risks to reporters covering Balochistan at Germany conference Spanish journalist Karlos Zurutuza has raised concerns over the limited international media coverage of Balochistan, highlighting the challenges faced by foreign correspondents and the growing risks confronting local journalists reporting on the region. ANI | Updated: 17-11-2026 14:51 IST | Created: 17-11-2026 14:51 IST

Representational Image (File photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Spanish journalist Karlos Zurutuza has raised concerns over the limited international media coverage of Balochistan, highlighting the challenges faced by foreign correspondents and the growing risks confronting local journalists reporting on the region. Speaking at an event organised by the Baloch National Movement (BNM) in Hannover, Germany, to mark Baloch Martyrs’ Day, Zurutuza said Balochistan remains largely invisible in international media despite its strategic geographical location and serious concerns surrounding press freedom and journalist safety. According to a report shared by the BNM in a post on X, Zurutuza said he could no longer travel to Balochistan and that opportunities to meet members of the Baloch community in Spain were limited. He explained that he intended to continue reporting on the region through remote interviews, telephone conversations and conferences while examining the reasons behind its limited international media visibility. Highlighting Balochistan's geographical and political significance, Zurutuza noted that the region borders Pakistan, Iran and Afghanistan, countries frequently covered by international media. However, he pointed out that the Baloch people, whom he described as direct targets of such groups, remain largely unfamiliar to international audiences. Addressing the challenges faced by foreign correspondents, Zurutuza cited instances of journalists being targeted, expelled or prevented from reporting independently in Balochistan. He referred to New York Times journalist Carlotta Gall, who, according to his account, was beaten and expelled in 2006, as well as another reporter who was expelled after publishing a single story. He added that even if he could safely return to the region, language barriers would make independent reporting difficult, as he does not speak Balochi, Urdu or Farsi. Relying on local fixers and translators, he warned, could expose those assisting foreign journalists to harassment, imprisonment and other serious consequences. Zurutuza also drew attention to the dangers faced by Baloch journalists and activists, referring to the cases of Karima Baloch, who died in Canada after going into exile, and a Baloch journalist whose body was found in Sweden. He said journalists working in the region have faced pressure on media editors, direct threats against their families and an environment that encourages self-censorship. Referring to Reporters Without Borders, he cited Pakistan's ranking of 153rd on the World Press Freedom Index and alleged that censorship in Balochistan had become increasingly bureaucratised, with media organisations facing requirements to obtain prior clearance before reporting on security forces. Citing figures attributed to Freedom Network, Zurutuza said at least 40 journalists had been killed in Balochistan over the past two decades, underlining the dangers associated with independent reporting in the region. He also mentioned the case of Baloch rights activist Mahrang Baloch, saying she had been in contact with him before her arrest and remained imprisoned despite receiving a Nobel Peace Prize nomination. Discussing possible ways to address the lack of international coverage, Zurutuza said journalists should focus on practical initiatives rather than limiting their efforts to appeals to the United Nations. He emphasised the importance of training local reporters in secure communication techniques and establishing professional networks that could help their reports reach international editors and media organisations willing to cover Balochistan. Concluding his remarks, Zurutuza underscored the importance of supporting local journalists and creating safer channels for independent reporting, arguing that greater international media attention was essential to bringing Balochistan's situation and the challenges faced by its people to a wider audience. (ANI)

item.title: Jumping genes may help brain cells produce wider variety of proteins: Study
item.description: Researchers at the University of Oxford have discovered that so-called "jumping genes" are frequently incorporated into genetic messages produced by cells in the fruit fly brain. In the examples ...
item.content:encoded:
Jumping genes may help brain cells produce wider variety of proteins: Study Researchers at the University of Oxford have discovered that so-called "jumping genes" are frequently incorporated into genetic messages produced by cells in the fruit fly brain. In the examples studied an average of almost one in five RNA messages contained sequence from a jumping gene. ANI | Updated: 17-11-2026 14:49 IST | Created: 17-11-2026 14:49 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Researchers at the University of Oxford have discovered that so-called "jumping genes" are frequently incorporated into genetic messages produced by cells in the fruit fly brain. In the examples studied, an average of almost one in five RNA messages contained sequence from a jumping gene. Scientists already knew that these mobile stretches of DNA, known as transposable elements (TEs), have played an important role in shaping animal genomes, sometimes becoming part of the RNA messages produced from genes. But the new study reveals that this happens particularly frequently in the brain, potentially giving brain cells another way to generate a greater variety of proteins. This new Oxford study used an improved computational method to measure how often TE sequences were included in messenger RNA in the fruit fly brain. Genes are often thought of as fixed instructions encoded within DNA. But before those instructions can be used, cells make a working copy called messenger RNA, or mRNA. Cells can edit these messages, cutting and joining different sections together through a process known as alternative splicing. This allows a single gene to produce different versions of an RNA message. During this editing process, TE sequences can also be incorporated into the message. These ancient pieces of DNA have spent more than a billion years copying themselves and spreading through animal genomes. Traditionally regarded as selfish genetic parasites, they have also left behind a vast reservoir of new genetic material that over evolutionary time could be reused. Studying these events is challenging because transposable elements are highly repetitive, making them difficult to analyse using standard approaches. The Oxford team used an improved computational analysis pipeline called TEChim, together with validation in the laboratory. Importantly, the improved method allowed the researchers to identify where jumping gene sequences were incorporated into RNA messages as well as measure how often the altered message was produced compared to the usual version. Across the 264 TE-gene pairs they tested, an average of 17.8 per cent of messenger RNA molecules contained TE-derived sequence, with some genes incorporating these sequences into nearly all of their transcripts. Dr. Christoph Treiber, Associate Professor in the Department of Biology at the University of Oxford, who led the study, said, “We knew these hybrid messages existed, but once we could measure how common they really were, the results really surprised us. On average, almost one in five RNA molecules from the genes we studied contained TE sequence. That’s far too frequent to dismiss as biological noise.” What makes this mechanism particularly interesting is that, unlike most genes, TEs vary considerably between individuals. This raises the possibility that two flies carrying different TE insertions may produce different versions of the same neural genes. Dr Treiber added, “TEs provide a source of entirely new genetic sequence that evolution can experiment with. And because these elements differ between individuals, they also have the potential to generate differences in the proteins produced by the brain, even between members of the same species.” Although the work was carried out in fruit flies, similar TE-containing RNA messages have been identified in mammals, including in humans. This raises the possibility that the incorporation of TE sequences into RNA could be a widespread way in which genomes expand the diversity of the proteins they can produce Dr Treiber and his team now hope to determine how these newly generated RNA variants produce new versions of proteins and how they affect brain function, whether different types of brain cells use different TE-derived sections, and whether variations in TEs contribute to differences between individuals. (ANI)

item.title: Dairy companies margins likely to improve in H2FY27 as milk procurement inflation peaks: Report
item.description: Profit margins of Indian dairy companies are expected to improve in the second half of FY27 as milk procurement inflation shows signs of peaking and recent price hikes begin to reflect fully in ...
item.content:encoded:
Dairy companies margins likely to improve in H2FY27 as milk procurement inflation peaks: Report Profit margins of Indian dairy companies are expected to improve in the second half of FY27 as milk procurement inflation shows signs of peaking and recent price hikes begin to reflect fully in earnings, according to a report by Yes Securities. ANI | Updated: 17-11-2026 14:42 IST | Created: 17-11-2026 14:42 IST

Representative image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Profit margins of Indian dairy companies are expected to improve in the second half of FY27 as milk procurement inflation shows signs of peaking and recent price hikes begin to reflect fully in earnings, according to a report by Yes Securities. The report noted that dairy companies could witness margin improvement even if milk procurement costs remain elevated, as recent increases in selling prices are expected to support profitability in the coming quarters. It highlighted that Q2FY27 marked the beginning of margin recovery for major dairy companies, despite an acceleration in milk procurement inflation, with revenue growth remaining strong and operating margins either holding steady or improving sequentially. "The reversal thesis is intact, but its mechanism has shifted from supply to price," it said, highlighting "Hikes were back-ended into September across the pack." Citing examples of major players, Yes Securities noted, Dodla Dairy increased prices by Rs 2.50 per litre, while Milky Mist implemented hikes of around 10 per cent, of which only 1.5-2 per cent was reflected in Q2 earnings. Meanwhile, major dairy cooperatives also raised prices. Aavin increased farm-gate prices by approximately Rs 6 per litre in August, while Karnataka Milk Federation (KMF) implemented an Rs 8 per litre consumer price hike from November 1. Similarly, Amul raised consumer milk prices by Rs 2-4 per litre from November 12, providing additional pricing flexibility to private dairy companies. "With procurement plateauing rather than softening into the flush, Q3FY27 should be the first quarter carrying full pass-through, keeping H2FY27 as the operative window," the report said. Beyond near-term profitability, there are growing opportunities for organised dairy companies as consumers increasingly shift towards branded and packaged products, it noted. "India's dairy market remains dominated by the unorganized segment, leaving a long runway for branded, packaged and cold-chain players," it said. The report highlighted that inflation in milk procurement costs appears to have "peaked" with prices stabilising across the dairy sector, while selling price increases implemented during Q2FY27 are expected to support margin recovery in the coming quarters. It further highlighted that dairy companies have already started witnessing an improvement in operating margins despite elevated procurement costs, indicating that recent price hikes are helping offset inflationary pressures. Further price increases by major dairy cooperatives have also provided additional flexibility for the organised dairy sector to pass on higher costs to consumers, it added. "H2FY27 should deliver a continued margin recovery on pricing alone, with further upside if the flush eases supply and demand for ghee and fats stays strong during the festive season," the report said. (ANI)
